meta.title: Who really said "I have come to the conclusion that one useless man is called a disgrace; that two are called a law firm; and that three or more become a Congress!"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not John Adams. The useless man / law firm / Congress joke was written for his stage character in the 1969 Broadway musical 1776, book by Peter Stone.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I have come to the conclusion that one useless man is called a disgrace; that two are called a law firm; and that three or more become a Congress!'?
meta.ogDescription: John Adams never said it. The joke opens the 1969 musical 1776, spoken by the stage Adams in Peter Stone's book, and was later mistaken for the real thing.

answer.label: Not John Adams — actually the musical 1776 (Peter Stone)
answer.sourceLine: This is dialogue for the character John Adams in the Broadway musical 1776 (opened 1969; book by Peter Stone, music and lyrics by Sherman Edwards). The real Adams (1735–1826) never said it. Quote collections later presented the stage joke as his own words, often reworded as “one useless man is a shame, two is a law firm, and three or more is a congress.”

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from
source.excerpt: ADAMS: I have come to the conclusion that one useless man is called a disgrace; that two are called a law firm; and that three or more become a Congress! And by God, I have had this Congress!
trail: Wikiquote’s John Adams page lists the line under Misattributed, noting it is Adams “as portrayed in the musical 1776 (1969)”: Wikiquote: John Adams ↗

Barry Popik (2009) says Adams “never said it.” He quotes the script transcript and a Cleveland Press review of 2 February 1971 describing the stage Adams opening the show with the joke: barrypopik.com ↗

Popik also records the reworded “one useless man is a shame, two is a law firm, and three or more is a congress” printed as Adams’s own words in The Quotable John Adams (Lyons Press, 2008), p. 207: barrypopik.com ↗
Peter Stone wrote the book of 1776, which opened on Broadway on 16 March 1969. The libretto was published by Viking in 1970: Wikipedia: 1776 (musical) ↗ · Encyclopedia.com: Peter Stone ↗
source.cutTag: Spoken by the stage John Adams to open the show
source.excerptNote: The wording follows the script transcript quoted by Barry Popik and Wikiquote. Wikiquote’s page for the 1972 film punctuates it with commas instead of semicolons. We did not check the page of the printed 1970 libretto.

source.rightsNote: The line comes from the musical 1776, staged in 1969. Its libretto was first published by Viking in 1970. Because that is after 1931, the text is still in copyright in the US, held by the authors’ estates and publisher. Quoting one line, as here, is a short excerpt for commentary.

author.name: Peter Stone
author.heading: About Peter Stone
author.metaLine: 1930–2003 · American playwright & screenwriter, book writer of 1776
author.bio: Peter Stone (born Los Angeles, 1930; died New York, 2003) wrote the book of the Broadway musical 1776, which won the Tony Award for Best Musical. He also adapted it into the 1972 film. His other work includes an Oscar-winning screenplay for Father Goose (1964) and Tony-winning books for Woman of the Year and Titanic.

misattribution.heading: How a stage joke became a Founding Father quote
misattribution.intro: The joke is so in character for the prickly Adams of the musical that many readers now take it for the real man’s words. It is often reworded on the way.

items.why: The historical Adams did not say it. It is dialogue for his character in the 1969 musical 1776, as both Wikiquote ↗ and Barry Popik ↗ document.

This book prints “In my many years I have come to a conclusion that one useless man is a shame, two is a law firm, and three or more is a congress” as Adams’s own words (p. 207), according to Popik ↗.
The Timpanogos blog says the line should be credited to the book writer: “Playwright Peter Stone wrote the witticism attributed to John Adams.” Timpanogos ↗

misattribution.truthLine: It is a line from the Broadway musical 1776 (1969), spoken by the stage John Adams. The book was by Peter Stone. It is not from any letter, diary or speech of the real Adams. Wikiquote ↗

context.heading: Why it sounds like Adams
lead: 1776 dramatizes the Continental Congress debating independence. It casts John Adams as the delegate “obnoxious and disliked” by his colleagues. The show opens with Adams venting at Congress’s inaction, and in the opening number, “Sit Down, John,” the other delegates tell him to sit down. A Cleveland Press review of 1971, quoted by Barry Popik ↗, says the tone for the evening is set when Adams steps out and delivers this joke.
The real Adams did complain about Congress in his letters, so the line feels in character. That is why it travels so easily. But the wording is the musical’s, not the eighteenth century’s.
context.pull: A line written for an actor playing Adams, not one Adams wrote.
